why_how.text: A quick check of tires, seat, mirrors and gauges before moving prevents problems that are hard to fix once you are on the road.

scenario.text: Before a long weekend drive, Maya puts a penny head-down in the shallowest groove of her tire and can see all of Lincoln's head.

reasoning.text: The tread is safe only if it covers some part of Lincoln's head in the shallowest groove.

result.text: Her tread is too shallow, so grip in bad conditions would be sharply reduced and the tires need attention before the trip.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking tires only need a look once a year at service time.

correction.text: Tires should be inspected for wear and damage once a month or before a long trip.

memory_support.text: Seat, glass, belts, mirrors, then gauges, look and listen.

prompt.text: You have just started the engine. What should you check and do before pulling away?

answer.text: Check the fuel gauge and warning lights, keep the stereo low, use lights or wipers if needed, then stop, look and listen.

rationale.text: Once the engine runs, the gauges, warning lights and controls come first, and before moving you stop, look and listen for traffic, cyclists and pedestrians.

narration.text: This lesson opens the chapter on driving safely with a short routine for getting ready. Before you even turn the key, a few checks of the tires, the seat, the glass, the belts and the mirrors make the drive safer. After the engine starts, a second set of checks covers the gauges, warning lights and controls, and then a final look around before you move. None of these steps takes long, but skipping them is how many avoidable problems begin. We will go through the tire checks first, then the steps before and after starting the engine.

lines.text: Check pressure with a gauge before getting in.
Inspect tires monthly or before long trips.
Use the penny test for tread.

narration.text: Check tire pressure with a gauge before getting in, using the recommended pressure from the owner's manual or the driver's side door jamb, and adjust it if needed. Inspect tires for wear and damage once a month or before a long trip. In the penny test, place a penny head-down in the shallowest groove: if the tread covers any part of Lincoln's head, the tread depth is safe. Less tread than that sharply reduces grip in bad conditions, so worn tires are more than a cosmetic problem; they change how well the car stops and steers.

lines.text: Set the seat for view and reach.
Clean the glass; buckle everyone up.
Check you feel calm; adjust mirrors.

narration.text: Before starting the engine, set the seat so you have a clear view and can easily reach every control. Clean the windshield and windows. Buckle up yourself and make sure your passengers are buckled too. Check that you feel calm and ready to drive, because your state of mind is part of being prepared. Finally, adjust the rear and side mirrors so they show what you need to see. Doing these steps in the same order every time turns them into a habit, and a habit is much harder to forget than a list you try to remember on a busy morning.

lines.text: Inspect tires monthly or before trips.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Many drivers think of tires as something a mechanic checks once in a while. The handbook asks more of you: inspect tires for wear and damage once a month or before a long trip, and check the pressure with a gauge before getting in. The penny test is a simple way to check tread at home. If you can see all of Lincoln's head in the shallowest groove, the tread is too shallow. Leaving tire checks to an annual service visit means you could drive for months on tires that no longer grip well in rain or snow.

Here is a quick check: you have just started the engine. What should you check and do before pulling away? Name the steps before reading on. Check the fuel gauge and the warning lights. Keep the stereo low enough to hear traffic. Switch on the headlights, the turn signal or the wipers if you need them. Then, before moving, stop, look and listen for traffic, cyclists and pedestrians. Only after that final look around should the car begin to move, because the checks before starting cannot tell you who is walking or riding nearby right now.

lines.text: Before starting: seat, glass, belts, mirrors.
After starting: gauges, then look and listen.

narration.text: To review, check tire pressure with a gauge before getting in and inspect the tires for wear once a month or before a long trip, using the penny test for tread depth. Before starting the engine, set the seat, clean the glass, buckle up everyone, make sure you feel calm and adjust the mirrors. After starting, check the fuel gauge and warning lights, keep the stereo low, use lights, signals or wipers as needed, and stop, look and listen before you move. Next we turn to the language of signs: their purposes, colors and shapes.

why_how.text: Signs use set colors and shapes so a driver can read the message at a glance, even before the words are visible.
Orange diamonds mark work areas, where lanes, speeds and fines all change.

scenario.text: A driver sees a yellow diamond with black symbols far ahead on a rural road.

reasoning.text: Warning signs are yellow diamonds with black letters or symbols, and yellow is the general warning color.

result.text: The driver knows a hazard is ahead and prepares to slow down before reading the details.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the round railroad sign and the X-shaped crossbuck mean the same thing.

correction.text: The round sign warns that a crossing is ahead, while the crossbuck marks where the tracks actually are.

memory_support.text: Eight sides stop, five sides school, diamonds warn.

prompt.text: You see an orange diamond on the highway. What does it most likely tell you?

answer.text: Road work is ahead, so slow down and follow the posted signs and any flaggers.

rationale.text: Orange warns of construction or repair, most work-area signs are diamonds, and drivers must slow and obey signs and flaggers.

narration.text: Traffic signs speak a visual language. They serve three purposes: to regulate, to warn and to inform. Their shapes and colors carry set meanings, so you can understand the message quickly, often before you can read any words. In this lesson we will learn what each color means, what each shape means, how regulatory and warning signs are told apart, what route markers look like, and how work areas are marked with signs, cones, drums and barricades. Learning the colors and shapes together lets you read most signs from a distance at a glance.

lines.text: Red: stop, no or do not.
Orange, blue, brown: work, services, recreation.

narration.text: Each sign color has a fixed meaning. Red means stop, no or do not. Green gives direction or guidance. Yellow or yellow-green is a general warning. White marks a regulation, law or rule. Orange warns of road construction or repair. Blue points to driver services such as food and lodging. Brown marks recreation and scenic information. If you can only see the color of a sign in the distance, you already know what kind of message to expect, whether it is a rule to follow, a warning to slow down for, or simply information about where to find services.

lines.text: Rectangle: rules or directions. Inverted triangle: yield.

narration.text: Shapes carry meaning too. An eight-sided octagon means stop. A diamond means warning. A rectangle gives regulations or directions. An inverted triangle means yield right-of-way. A pennant means no passing. A five-sided pentagon marks school zones and school crossings. A circle warns of a railroad crossing ahead, while a crossbuck marks the crossing itself. A shield is a route marker. Route signs are usually shields, though their shapes and colors vary, and they show US, Interstate and state route numbers. Each shape is reserved, so it means the same thing wherever you see it.

lines.text: Regulatory: white rectangles you must obey.
Warning: yellow diamonds with black symbols.

narration.text: Two of the most common sign families are easy to tell apart. Regulatory signs are rectangles with a white background, and they must be obeyed, because they state a law. Warning signs are yellow diamonds with black letters or symbols, and they alert you to hazards ahead, such as a curve or a merge. Putting color and shape together helps: a white rectangle is a rule, a yellow diamond is a warning. That way, even before you read the words, you know whether the sign is telling you what you must do or what you should watch out for.

lines.text: Slow down; obey signs and flaggers.

narration.text: Work areas have their own signs and devices. Most work-area signs are diamond-shaped, and orange is the color that warns of construction or repair. In a work zone, drivers must slow down and obey the posted signs and any flaggers, and violations in work zones carry increased fines. Cones, drums and barricades steer drivers through the work area, and they can carry warning lights for night work. Slowing down and following the flaggers is what the law expects of every driver passing through. Fines are higher there. Stay alert.

lines.text: Circle ahead, crossbuck at the tracks.
Pentagon for school, pennant for no passing.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from shapes that are easy to confuse. Both the circle and the crossbuck relate to trains, but the round sign warns that a crossing is ahead, while the X-shaped crossbuck marks where the tracks actually are. Another pair is the pentagon and the pennant. The five-sided pentagon is the school-zone and school-crossing shape, whereas the pennant is the no-passing shape. When a question describes a shape in words, slow down and count the sides or picture the outline before answering, because the look-alike shape usually appears as a wrong option.

lines.text: An orange diamond on the highway.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on the highway you see an orange diamond. What is it most likely telling you, and what should you do? Recall the color and the shape before reading on. Orange warns of road construction or repair, and most work-area signs are diamond-shaped. So road work is ahead. Slow down, obey the posted signs and follow any flaggers. Remember that violations in work zones carry increased fines, and that cones, drums and barricades may steer you through the area, sometimes with warning lights at night. The color and the shape agree.

lines.text: Colors and shapes carry set meanings.
White rectangles rule; yellow diamonds warn.

narration.text: To sum up, signs regulate, warn and inform. Red means stop, green guides, yellow warns, white states a rule, orange marks road work, blue points to services and brown marks recreation. The octagon means stop, the diamond warns, the rectangle gives rules or directions, the inverted triangle means yield, the pennant means no passing, the pentagon marks schools, the circle warns of a crossing ahead, the crossbuck marks the tracks and the shield marks a route. In work zones, slow down, obey signs and flaggers, and expect higher fines. Next we look at stop and yield rules.

why_how.text: Stop and yield signs decide who goes first, and getting them wrong is a common cause of crashes at intersections.
Emergency vehicles need a clear path, so the law tells drivers exactly where to pull over and stop.

scenario.text: Two cars reach a four-way stop; the other car stopped first, and a third car is already crossing.

reasoning.text: At a four-way stop, wait for vehicles already in the intersection and let those that arrived before you go first.

result.text: Let the crossing car finish, let the earlier car go, then take your turn.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a yield sign always requires a full stop, just like a stop sign.

correction.text: A yield sign lets you keep moving without a full stop when it is safe; you slow down and yield to others.

memory_support.text: Stop means stop; yield means slow and give way.

prompt.text: A fire engine with siren and red lights comes up behind you while you are halfway through an intersection. Where do you stop?

answer.text: Past the intersection, at the right edge of the road.

rationale.text: Pull to the right edge and stop until the emergency vehicle passes, but never stop inside an intersection.

narration.text: This lesson covers the signs and situations that decide who stops and who goes. We will look at exactly where to stop at a stop sign, what to do when there is no stop line, how a four-way stop works, and how a yield sign differs from a stop sign. Then we turn to emergency vehicles, which take priority whenever their siren and red lights are on. Each of these rules is about sharing the intersection safely, and each one comes up again and again in everyday driving, so it pays to know them well. Each rule protects someone at the intersection.

lines.text: Stop fully behind the crosswalk or line.
Hidden cross street: ease forward slowly.
No line: stop where you can see.

narration.text: At a stop sign, stop completely behind the crosswalk or the stop line. If the cross street is hidden, ease forward slowly until you can tell it is safe. Where there is no stop line or crosswalk, slow down and stop if needed at the point closest to the intersection that gives you a view of oncoming through traffic. Then yield to pedestrians and cross traffic before going. The idea is the same in every case: a full stop first, at the right place, and then enough of a view to see what is coming before you enter the intersection.

lines.text: Four-way: those already in, then earlier arrivals.
Yield: slow, give way, keep moving if safe.

narration.text: At a four-way stop, wait for any vehicles already in the intersection and let vehicles that arrived before you go first. A yield sign works like a stop sign, except you may keep moving without a full stop when it is safe. At a yield sign, slow down and yield to pedestrians, through traffic, drivers already on the highway, and vehicles making a U-turn. If someone is coming, you stop and wait; if the way is clear, you continue at a safe speed. So the yield sign asks for judgment, while the stop sign always asks for a full stop.

lines.text: Stop sign: always a full stop.
Yield sign: stop only if needed.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because a yield sign works like a stop sign in many ways, some drivers believe it always requires a full stop, and others treat it as no rule at all. Neither is right. A stop sign always requires a full stop. A yield sign requires you to slow down and yield, but it lets you continue without stopping when the way is clear. If pedestrians or traffic are coming, you must stop and let them go. So read the shape: the octagon always means stop, while the inverted triangle means slow down and give way. Read the shape first.

lines.text: A fire engine with siren and lights.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a fire engine with its siren and red lights on comes up behind you while you are halfway through an intersection. Where do you stop? Think about the rule before reading on. Do not stop inside the intersection. Continue through it carefully, then pull to the right edge of the road and stop until the emergency vehicle has passed. The same applies to police cars, ambulances and other emergency vehicles. Stopping in the intersection could block the path the emergency vehicle needs, which defeats the purpose of pulling over.

Let us sum up. At a stop sign, stop fully behind the crosswalk or stop line, ease forward if the cross street is hidden, and where no line exists stop where you can see oncoming traffic. At a four-way stop, vehicles already in the intersection go first, then those that arrived before you. A yield sign means slow down and give way, with a full stop only when needed. When an emergency vehicle approaches with siren and red lights, pull to the right edge and stop until it passes, but never stop inside an intersection. Next we look at traffic lights and arrows.

why_how.text: Every light and arrow tells you something different, and the differences between them decide whether you stop, yield or go.
Turning on red is legal in some cases and illegal in others, so the details matter at nearly every signal.

scenario.text: You approach an intersection as the light turns steady yellow, and you are still well short of the stop line.

reasoning.text: A steady yellow warns that red is coming: stop if you have not entered, clear the intersection if you have, and never speed up.

result.text: Because you have not entered the intersection, you stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a flashing yellow arrow gives you a protected left turn.

correction.text: A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians; a green arrow is the protected turn.

memory_support.text: Steady yellow stop, flashing yellow careful, flashing arrow yield.

prompt.text: You are on a one-way street at a red light and want to turn left onto another one-way street whose traffic flows left. May you?

answer.text: Yes, after signalling, stopping fully and yielding, unless a sign, arrow or officer forbids it.

rationale.text: Left on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street flowing left, after signalling, a full stop and yielding.

narration.text: This lesson covers the traffic signal in all its forms: steady lights, flashing lights, arrows, and what to do when the lights are dark. Each signal gives a different instruction, and several of them look alike, especially the yellow ones. We will also look at when you may turn right or left on a red light, because those rules differ sharply. By the end, you should be able to look at any signal and know whether it tells you to stop, to stop and then go, to yield, or to go ahead while still watching for pedestrians and other traffic.

lines.text: Red: stop behind the line until green.
Green: straight or turn, unless forbidden.

narration.text: At a red light, stop completely behind the crosswalk or stop line, or before entering the intersection if neither exists, and stay stopped until the light turns green. A steady yellow light warns that red is coming: stop if you have not entered the intersection, keep going and clear it if you already have, and never speed up to get through before red. A green light allows going straight, turning right or turning left, unless a sign forbids the turn. When lights are out, come to a full stop, yield to pedestrians and to vehicles already stopped or in the intersection, then proceed with caution.

lines.text: Flashing red: same as a stop sign.

narration.text: Flashing lights work differently from steady ones. A flashing red light means come to a full stop and go only when the road is clear and you have the right-of-way, exactly like a stop sign. A flashing yellow light means proceed with caution, without needing to stop. A dark, non-working signal is closest to the flashing red: both call for a full stop before proceeding. Keeping these straight matters, because a driver who treats a flashing red like a flashing yellow will roll into an intersection where cross traffic expects everyone to stop first.

lines.text: Red arrow: that movement is forbidden.

narration.text: Arrows control turns. A red arrow forbids the movement it points to, and drivers facing it must stop unless they are entering for a movement another signal allows. A steady yellow arrow warns that the arrow is about to turn red, so you should clear the intersection. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. A green arrow lets you go the way it points and protects the turn from other traffic, yet you must still yield to pedestrians, bicycles and vehicles already in the intersection when your arrow appears.

lines.text: Right on red: after a full stop, unless signed.
Left on red: one-way onto one-way only.

narration.text: Unless a sign prohibits it, you may turn right on red after a complete stop, signalling first and waiting until vehicles and pedestrians are clear. A left turn on red is much narrower. It is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street whose traffic flows to the left, after signalling, stopping fully and yielding, and only unless a sign, an arrow or an officer forbids it. So right on red is the broad rule, while left on red applies in just one situation. In both cases, the full stop comes first, and pedestrians and vehicles keep the right-of-way.

lines.text: Steady yellow light: stop if you can.
Flashing yellow light: go with caution.
Flashing yellow arrow: turn after yielding.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from three yellow signals. A steady yellow light means stop if you can before entering the intersection. A flashing yellow light means go ahead with caution. A flashing yellow arrow means turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. They share a color, but each gives a different instruction. A related trap is the flashing yellow arrow versus the green arrow: only the green arrow protects your turn from other traffic, while the flashing yellow arrow leaves you responsible for finding a safe gap before you turn.

Here is a quick check: you are stopped at a red light on a one-way street and want to turn left onto another one-way street whose traffic flows to the left. May you turn? Think about the narrow rule before reading on. Yes. A left turn on red is allowed in exactly this situation, after you signal, stop completely and yield to pedestrians and traffic, unless a sign, an arrow or an officer forbids it. If either street were a two-way street, the left turn on red would not be allowed, even though a right turn on red usually would be.

lines.text: Red stop, yellow warn, green go.
Flashing red and dark signals: full stop.
Turns on red follow strict rules.

narration.text: To review, stop behind the line at a red light until it turns green, stop at a steady yellow if you have not entered, and go on green unless a sign forbids a turn. A flashing red works like a stop sign, a flashing yellow means proceed with caution, and a dark signal means a full stop first. A red arrow forbids its movement, a steady yellow arrow says clear the intersection, a flashing yellow arrow says turn after yielding, and a green arrow protects the turn while you still yield to those already crossing. Right on red is broad; left on red is narrow.

why_how.text: Pedestrians have their own signals, and drivers must know them to yield at the right moment.
School zones and crossing guards protect children, and the rules carry exact hours and limits.

scenario.text: A pedestrian starts crossing as the hand begins flashing and a countdown shows eight.

reasoning.text: With a countdown timer, pedestrians may still start but must finish crossing before the count reaches zero.

result.text: The pedestrian may continue, and drivers must let the person reach the other side.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a green turn arrow also lets pedestrians cross.

correction.text: Pedestrians facing a green turn arrow may not cross unless a pedestrian signal or officer allows it.

memory_support.text: Countdown: start only if you can finish.

prompt.text: A school-zone sign has no special hours posted, and classes end at three. Until when does the lower limit apply?

answer.text: Until half an hour after classes end.

rationale.text: Unless posted otherwise, school-zone limits apply on school days from half an hour before classes start until half an hour after they end.

narration.text: This lesson covers the people who share the road without a vehicle. Pedestrians at intersections follow traffic lights and their own walk signals, and drivers must yield to them at the right moments. We will look at what each pedestrian signal means, where most pedestrian deaths happen, and then the rules around schools: crossing guards, school-zone speed limits and their hours, and when U-turns are banned near schools. Children are the hardest pedestrians to predict, so the school rules are written to give them extra protection.

Pedestrians at intersections must obey traffic signals, unless a pedestrian signal or an officer directs otherwise. On a red light they do not cross, on a yellow light they must not start across, and on a green light they may cross. Pedestrians facing a green turn arrow may not cross unless a pedestrian signal or an officer allows it, and where a crosswalk is marked they must use it. So the vehicle arrow is not a walking signal. Drivers should still watch for pedestrians who misread the lights, because a mistake at a crosswalk can be deadly.

A lit WALK sign or walking-person symbol lets pedestrians cross in the direction of the signal, and the drivers of all vehicles must give them the right-of-way. A flashing DON'T WALK or upraised hand with a countdown timer still lets pedestrians start, but they must finish crossing before the count reaches zero; without a countdown, a flashing hand means they may not start. A steady DON'T WALK or upraised hand means no pedestrian may start crossing, and anyone already lawfully in the road must get to a curb, sidewalk, safety zone or other safe place as soon as possible.

Intersections are not where most pedestrian deaths happen. Most happen mid-block, between intersections, where drivers may not expect anyone to cross. Both drivers and pedestrians share responsibility for safety, so drivers should always be ready to yield. That means watching the sidewalks and the gaps between parked cars, not just the crosswalks. A pedestrian who steps out mid-block may be breaking a rule, but avoiding the crash is still the driver's job, and lower speeds give you the time you need to react. Watch every gap.

lines.text: Disobeying a guard is a misdemeanor.
Wait until the guard fully leaves.
Limits: fifteen or twenty-five miles per hour.

narration.text: Disobeying a school crossing guard is a misdemeanor in Nevada, and drivers must wait until the guard has fully left the crosswalk. School-zone speed limits are fifteen or twenty-five miles per hour, and they apply on school days from half an hour before classes start until half an hour after they end, unless posted otherwise. If flashing yellow lights are off during class time, the regular limit applies. Some zones use flashing yellow lights to show when the lower limit is in effect, so the lights tell you directly when to slow down.

lines.text: Banned while the zone is in effect.
Allowed when no children are present.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Drivers sometimes assume a U-turn is fine anywhere it can be made safely. In a school zone, U-turns are banned, except when no children are present, on days without school, outside the half-hour windows around the school day, or when signs or lights show the zone is not in effect. So the ban follows the school schedule. A second trap is the speed limit itself: the lower limit applies from half an hour before classes to half an hour after, unless posted otherwise, not only while children are visible near the road.

Here is a quick check: a school zone has no special hours posted, and classes end at three in the afternoon. Until when does the lower school-zone limit apply? Work it out before reading on. It applies until half an hour after classes end, so until three thirty. On school days, unless posted otherwise, school-zone limits run from half an hour before classes start until half an hour after they end. If the zone uses flashing yellow lights and the lights are off during class time, the regular limit applies instead. The clock decides.

lines.text: Pedestrians follow lights and walk signals.
School-zone limits follow the school day.

narration.text: Let us review. Pedestrians obey traffic lights unless a pedestrian signal or officer directs otherwise, and a green turn arrow is not a walk signal. A WALK signal gives them the right-of-way, a flashing hand with a countdown lets them start only if they can finish, and a steady hand means no one starts. Most pedestrian deaths happen mid-block, so always be ready to yield. Wait until a crossing guard fully leaves the crosswalk. School-zone limits of fifteen or twenty-five miles per hour apply around the school day, and U-turns there are banned while the zone is in effect.

why_how.text: Lane lines tell you where you may drive, change lanes and pass, even when no sign is in view.

scenario.text: On a two-lane road you see double yellow lines: a broken line on your side and a solid line on the other side.

reasoning.text: With double yellow lines, you may not pass if the line on your side is solid; a broken yellow line allows passing when safe.

result.text: Because your side is broken, you may pass when it is safe, while drivers coming the other way may not.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a center left-turn lane can be used to pass slow traffic.

correction.text: A center left-turn lane may be crossed only to turn left onto or off the highway and is never a travel or passing lane.

memory_support.text: White same way, yellow opposite; solid means stay.

prompt.text: You turn left onto a highway into the center turn lane. How far may you drive in it before merging?

rationale.text: You may drive no more than two hundred feet in a center turn lane before turning left, and no more than fifty feet after turning onto the highway before merging.

narration.text: Pavement markings guide you even where no sign stands. Markings are white or yellow, and each color and style has a meaning. In this lesson we cover broken and solid white lines, broken, solid and double yellow lines, crosswalks, stop lines and dotted lines, and the center left-turn lane with its distance limits. Once you know the system, a quick look at the lines tells you which way traffic is flowing, whether you may change lanes, and whether you may pass. That makes markings one of the most useful things to read correctly at speed.

lines.text: Broken white: lanes moving the same way.
Solid white: no lane changes or passing.

narration.text: Broken white lines divide lanes moving the same way. Stay inside your lane without straddling the line, and pass only when it is safe. A solid white line between same-direction lanes means no lane changes and no passing. Solid white lines also mark the highway edge and the line between a travel lane and the shoulder. Stop lines are wide white lines across a lane where you stop with a view of traffic from every direction, and dotted white lines either carry a lane line through an intersection or mark freeway exit-only lanes.

lines.text: Solid yellow: do not cross or pass.

narration.text: Yellow lines divide traffic moving in opposite directions. A broken yellow line allows passing when it is safe. A solid yellow line means do not cross or pass, and solid yellow also marks the left edge of multi-lane divided highways. With double yellow lines, you may not pass if the line on your side is solid. So when you see yellow, you know that the traffic on the other side of it is coming toward you, which is why the passing rules for yellow lines are stricter than the rules for white lane lines. Yellow always means opposing traffic.

lines.text: Yield even where none is painted.
Center turn lane: left turns only.

narration.text: Always stop before a crosswalk, and at intersections where no crosswalk is painted you must still yield to pedestrians. A center left-turn lane is edged by solid and broken yellow lines. It may be crossed only to turn left onto or off the highway, and it is never a travel or passing lane. You may drive no more than two hundred feet in a center turn lane before turning left, and no more than fifty feet in it after turning onto the highway before merging into traffic. Those two distances keep the lane free for its real purpose: left turns.

lines.text: Solid lines mean stay in place.

narration.text: Here is a trap with colors and styles. White lane lines separate same-direction traffic and white markings also mark road edges, shoulders, crosswalks and stop lines, whereas yellow lines separate opposite-direction traffic. Within white lines, broken white separates same-direction lanes and allows passing when safe, while solid white between same-direction lanes forbids lane changes and passing. Within yellow lines, broken allows passing when safe and solid forbids it. Answer marking questions in two steps: first the color, which tells you the direction of the other traffic, then the style, which tells you whether you may cross the line.

Here is a quick check: you turn left onto a highway and enter the center turn lane to wait for a gap. How far may you drive in that lane before merging into traffic? Recall the two distances before reading on. No more than fifty feet. The longer distance, two hundred feet, is the limit for driving in the center turn lane before turning left off the highway. In both cases the lane is only for left turns, and it may never be used as a travel lane or to pass slower vehicles, no matter how open it looks. Keep the two numbers apart.

lines.text: Solid lines: no crossing or passing.
Center turn lane: left turns, short distances.

narration.text: Let us review. Pavement markings are white or yellow. Broken white lines divide same-direction lanes, and solid white forbids lane changes and marks edges and shoulders. Yellow lines divide opposite directions: broken yellow allows passing when safe, solid yellow forbids it, and with double yellow you may not pass when the solid line is on your side. Stop before crosswalks and yield to pedestrians even where none is painted. Stop lines are wide white lines, dotted lines carry lanes through intersections or mark exit lanes, and the center turn lane is for left turns only.

why_how.text: A train cannot stop in time to avoid a car, so the rules at crossings leave no room for guessing.
Knowing what to do if your car stalls on the tracks can save your life.

scenario.text: Crossing lights are flashing and the gate is down, but a driver sees no train in either direction.

reasoning.text: Never drive around a lowered crossing gate, even if no train is visible.

result.text: The driver stays stopped until the gate rises, because a lowered gate means a train is coming.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking it is safe to go around a lowered gate when no train is in sight.

correction.text: Never drive around a lowered gate even if no train is visible; at flashing lights, stop and go only when it is safe.

memory_support.text: Fifteen feet to stop, fifty feet to park.

prompt.text: Your car stalls on the tracks with a crossing ahead of you. What do you do first?

rationale.text: If your vehicle stalls on the tracks, get out immediately, find the blue Emergency Notification System sign and notify the railroad and local police.

narration.text: This lesson covers railroad crossings, where a mistake can be fatal because a train cannot stop in time to avoid a car. We will look at what railroad crossing signs ask of you, where to stop when a train is coming, which vehicles must always stop, how to treat gates and flashing lights, how far from the tracks you may park, what to do at crossings with several tracks, and what to do if your vehicle stalls on the tracks. Throughout, the rule is the same: the train has the right-of-way, every time, and you yield to it.

lines.text: Slow, look both ways, stay off.
Stop sign at the crossing: stop.
Train coming: stop fifteen feet back.

narration.text: Railroad crossing signs warn you to slow down and possibly stop. Look both ways, and stay off the tracks whenever a train is approaching. At a railroad crossing with a stop sign, you must stop. When a train is coming, you must stop at least fifteen feet from the tracks. Passenger buses and trucks hauling flammable or dangerous materials must stop at railroad crossings even when no signal shows and no train is coming. A crossbuck means drivers must yield to trains, and a train's speed is hard to judge. Always yield to the train.

lines.text: Never drive around a lowered gate.
Flashing lights: stop, go only when safe.
Several tracks: wait for a clear view.

narration.text: Never drive around a lowered crossing gate, even if no train is visible. When crossing lights flash, you must stop, and you may go only if no train is visible or it is safe. At a crossing with more than one set of tracks, wait for a clear view in both directions before starting across, looking both ways each time. Never shift gears while on the tracks, since a stalled engine at the wrong moment leaves you stuck in the train's path. Keep moving steadily once you start across. A lowered gate always means stay put, however empty the tracks look.

lines.text: Stop at least fifteen feet away.
Park no closer than fifty feet.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two distances apply near railroad tracks, and they are easy to swap. When a train is coming, you stop at least fifteen feet from the tracks. When you park, you may never park within fifty feet of the nearest rail of a railroad. The smaller number is about where you wait for a passing train; the larger number is about where a parked car may sit. If a question asks about parking, think fifty. If it asks where to stop for an approaching train, think fifteen, and remember that more distance is always allowed.

lines.text: Your car stalls on the tracks.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: your car stalls on the railroad tracks. What do you do first, and what next? Decide before reading on. First, get out at once. Do not stay inside trying to restart the engine. Next, find the blue Emergency Notification System sign at the crossing and notify the railroad and the local police, so a train can be warned. A train cannot stop in time to avoid a car, which is why leaving the vehicle immediately matters more than trying to save it. Your safety comes before the car every time. Leave the car behind.

lines.text: Fifteen feet to stop, fifty to park.

narration.text: To review, railroad crossing signs mean slow down, look both ways and stay off the tracks when a train approaches. Stop at a crossing with a stop sign, and stop at least fifteen feet from the tracks when a train is coming. Buses and hazardous-material trucks always stop. Never drive around a lowered gate, and at flashing lights go only when safe. Wait for a clear view at multiple tracks and never shift gears on them. Never park within fifty feet of the nearest rail. If you stall, get out at once and use the blue sign to call the railroad and police.
